newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Working population does not include family caregiver.
newsitem.headline: Working population does not include family caregiver.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday Community rules requiring equal treatment between men and women do not extend to unemployed spouses providing nursing care for husbands at home.
After a German citizen, Mr Zuchner, became paraplegic from an accident, he required both general care and therapeutic treatment.
His wife sought financial assistance for therapeutic treatment under German law, but was found ineligible because she was available to care for her husband.

Mrs Zuchner appealed the decision arguing it violated Community rules guaranteeing equal treatment of men and women. The court looked first at whether Mrs Zuchner fell under the definition of "working population."

The working populaton, according to the directive, includes self-employed persons or persons whose activity is interrupted by invalidity. Mrs Zuchner was not working when her husband had the accident, but argued she underwent training to care for her husband and if she didn't do it, someone or a hospital would be paid to care for her husband.

The European Commission supported Mrs Zuchner's position, but Britain and Germany disagreed. They argued caregivers cannot be considered a member of the working population merely because of the extent of the care provided.

The court maintained that the concept of "working population" is very wide and "includes people who are working, those who are seeking employment and those whose work or efforts to find work have been interrupted by materialization of any of the risks mentioned in the directive."

"On the other hand, the directive does not apply to people who are not working and are not seeking work or to persons whose occupation or efforts to find work were not interrupted by one of the risk identified in the directive," the court said.

Mrs Zuchner fell into that category. The court reasoned that to include within the working population family members working for the benefit of another family member would "infinitely extend the scope of the directive" beyond its intent.
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: German)
"Equal treatment for men and women in matters of social security - Directive 79/7/EEC - Working poplulation"
Reference from the Hanseatisches Oberlandesgericht, Bremen, Germany for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings pending bfore that court between

on the interpretation of Council directive 79/7/EEC of 19 December 1978 on the progressive implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of social security (OJ 1979 L 6, p. 24), and of the principles of Community law governing the liability of public authorities

Article 2 of Council directive 79/7/EEC of 19 December 1978 on the progressive implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of social security must be interpreted as not covering a person who undertakes, as an unremunerated activity, the care of his or her handicapped spouse, whatever the extent of that activity and the competence required in order to perform it, where the person in question did not, in order to do so, abandon an occupatonal activity or interrupt efforts to find employment.
